claims.statement: MCM is a polyglot pnpm/Nx monorepo comprising a React Native/Expo universal client, a Rust/Axum domain service, a Python LangGraph agent gateway, three scoped MCP servers, shared infrastructure-as-code, and a self-hosted Forgejo CI/CD pipeline.
All build, test, and lint tasks in the MCM monorepo are invoked through Nx as the universal task runner; npm/yarn and the underlying tools (cargo, pytest, etc.) are never run directly.

The primary AI-assisted development environment is a dev container hosted inside a Docker Sandbox microVM (feature 060), not Docker-in-Docker. Sibling containers build on the microVM's own engine and share its network namespace (`docker-outside-of-docker`, `--network=host`); egress is enforced by a deny-by-default policy outside the VM.
The sandbox microVM path measured 0.43× the wall-clock of the Docker-in-Docker path across five bring-up stages; `docker-build` alone went from 1024 s to 293 s.

The one-step entry to the sandbox dev environment is `./scripts/open-sandbox.ps1`, which runs on Windows PowerShell 5.1 (not pwsh), checks whether the sandbox is running, starts it if not, waits for SSH, and opens VS Code directly inside the dev container.

The Docker Desktop / Docker-in-Docker dev container is retained solely for the Android emulator, which needs `/dev/kvm` that the microVM cannot provide (feature 060, gate R2, resolved negative). Everything else — web E2E, integration, the agent stack, day-to-day assistant work — belongs on the sandbox. Its entry point is VS Code's *Dev Containers: Clone Repository in Named Container Volume* command against `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json`.

AI-assisted coding (Claude Code) runs on the Claude MAX subscription. `MCM_ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is mapped to `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` only at the point of use in three separate processes (`agent-stack.mjs`, `wiki-maintain.mjs`, containerized E2E). Setting `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` in any environment silently bills pay-per-token; this was measured at ~$15 unintended spend in one day (2026-08-16).

Before writing implementation code under `backend/`, `frontend/`, `agents/`, `mcp-servers/`, or `infrastructure-as-code/`, a numbered `specs/NNN-*/` spec → plan → tasks set must already exist. Proposals and knowledge/index edits are exempt.

A PR's head must be a real branch (`git push origin HEAD:<branch>`), not an AGit push (`HEAD:refs/for/main`). An AGit push yields a `refs/pull/N/head` head that Forgejo runs with NO Actions secrets — every `${{ secrets.* }}` is empty. This cost two sessions on issue #126.
`sbx start` is not a valid command — it silently prints the root help. To restart a stopped sandbox, use `sbx run --name mcm -d`.
`--name` is load-bearing on `sbx run` because the first positional argument is an agent, not a sandbox name. Omitting it can create a second sandbox instead of restarting the existing one.

`sandboxd` does not auto-start at boot. `sbx run --name mcm -d` starts it on demand. Reaching for `ssh mcm.sbx` before starting it surfaces a daemon error that reads like a broken environment rather than a cold host.

`sbx template save` snapshots the VM root filesystem, not the Docker data disk, so a sandbox recreated from a template starts with zero images. The egress policy is also not carried in a template — a recreated sandbox gets the default profile and must have its policy re-applied.

`sbx run` mounts the current directory as the sandbox workspace over virtiofs, read-write, unless an explicit path is given. Creating a sandbox from inside the repo mounts the repo into the VM. Measured 2026-08-16: a file written inside a recreated sandbox appeared immediately in the Windows working copy.

The `docker-outside-of-docker` feature fronts the VM socket with a socat relay whose half-close timeout defaults to 0.5 s. `docker exec` half-closes stdin immediately, so socat tears the relay down mid-response — fast commands return exit 0 with no output, and the seam looks healthy under any quick probe while real work fails. The fix is to set `DOCKER_HOST=unix:///var/run/docker-host.sock`, already applied in `.devcontainer/sandbox/devcontainer.json`; contexts that do not inherit `containerEnv` must pass it explicitly. `verify-engine-seam.sh` guards it with a deliberately slow (2 s) probe, since a fast one would assert nothing.

In the sandbox, the in-VM firewall (`ipset`/`iptables`) is not used; enforcement is the host-side policy outside the VM, and triage order is therefore host policy first, in-VM second — the opposite of the Docker Desktop path. The in-VM layer is not merely unused but hazardous there: under `--network=host` the container shares the VM's network namespace identically, so a default-DROP would be VM-wide. `nc -z <ip> 443` reports OPEN against a blocked destination because the proxy accepts TCP and refuses at TLS; from the dev container a refusal is `rc=6` (NXDOMAIN) with `curl` writing `000`, so the exit code, not the status code, is the signal.

Git must run inside the dev container, not in the VM shell. The VM user and container user previously had different UIDs (uid 1000 vs a different uid), causing git writes from the VM shell to be unwritable by the container user. Fixed 2026-08-17: `toolchain.Dockerfile` now creates `coder` at 1000:1000.

Every `containerEnv` entry in a devcontainer.json becomes an `ENV` instruction in the generated derived image, making it permanently readable in `Config.Env` and history layers. Measured on the derived image on 2026-09-19: all four credential values were present in `Config.Env` and in three history layers. Credentials must go through the runtime env file written by `.devcontainer/gen-container-secrets-env.sh`, not declared in `containerEnv`.

`sbx` is pinned at v0.47.0 (`0411f50ee4700fe7bd37e6e7e3aced563e850ca9`), upgraded from v0.43.0 on 2026-10-08 via `winget upgrade Docker.sbx` after `sbx daemon stop`. Because it enforces this environment's isolation and egress, an upgrade is a security-relevant change with a required ritual: read the intervening release notes for network-policy, `--network=host`, port-publishing, idle-stop, secret-injection and template changes; capture the before-state with `verify-reboot-survival.sh --capture`; re-run the harness (`run-harness.sh`) plus the host-side `verify-sandbox-egress.sh --audit-check`; re-run the G5 sibling-egress refusal explicitly; and record the new version in the runbook. Several behaviours here are version-specific and undocumented.

`sbx run` can report `docker daemon failed to start inside the sandbox` while dockerd is healthy: restoring this VM's 20 `restart: unless-stopped` containers takes 54–101 s and overruns sbx's compiled-in dockerd-readiness budget, so sbx aborts, the CLI exits, and the ~30 s idle-stop kills a working VM. There is no knob (no flag, `DOCKER_SANDBOXES_*`/`SBX_*` variable, settings file, or daemon option; v0.43.0 did not raise it). `scripts/open-sandbox.ps1` works around it by treating the exit code as a claim and SSH answering as evidence, waiting up to a 120 s deadline; a bare `sbx run` still shows the false failure.

The sandbox microVM idle-stops roughly 30 seconds after the last session disconnects — hardcoded, with no configuration knob. A "missing" environment usually just idle-stopped and nothing is lost, but long unattended jobs die unless a session is held (`ssh mcm.sbx 'sleep 5400'` in another window, work launched with `setsid nohup … &`); the dev container returns by itself via `--restart=always`, while the agent stack deliberately does not.

In `sbx` v0.47.0 the VM-shell egress refusal body changed to HTTP 403 `Approval required for <host>:<port>.` (from `Blocked by network policy`). A harness check keyed to the old marker reported a deny-by-default breach that had not occurred, so both verify scripts (`verify-sandbox-egress.sh` and `verify-firewall-allowlist.sh`) now accept both bodies. The new body also queues a pending approval (`sbx policy approval ls`), and `sbx policy approval respond … allow` is a second path that widens egress while bypassing the canonical `.devcontainer/egress-allowlist.json` — it must never be used; add the destination to the canonical file and apply the generated rule instead, and use `dismiss` to clear the queue.

Because several concurrent Claude sessions can share `/workspaces/mcm` and its git index and checked-out branch (five were measured on 2026-09-18), any branch work must happen in a git worktree under `/home/coder/worktrees/<slug>`, never `/workspaces/.worktrees/…` (`/workspaces` is not writable). The `node_modules` symlink into the main checkout suffices for `node --test` and the `scripts/*.mjs` gates but not for any `pnpm nx` target, which fails with `ERR_PNPM_UNSAFE_MODULES_DIR` and needs a real `CI=true pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` inside the worktree; an nx failure whose message names a path that no longer exists is a stale-cache answer and must be re-run with `--skip-nx-cache` before diagnosis; and a worktree does not survive a container rebuild, so branches must be pushed before risky container operations.

The sandbox dev container's credentials are passed with `docker run --env-file` wired through `runArgs`, with the file written by `.devcontainer/gen-container-secrets-env.sh` as `initializeCommand` — which the devcontainer CLI runs on the VM before create, because `--env-file` fails on a missing file. `docker exec` still inherits the values and the image does not, but they remain visible in `docker inspect <container>`; `remoteEnv` is not usable here because it does not reach `ssh mcm.sbx` + `docker exec`. `devcontainer up` does not recreate the container when only `runArgs`/`containerEnv` change — it reattaches and reports success while the old image keeps running — so `--remove-existing-container` is required and verification must inspect the container rather than the command's exit code.

The sandbox operating manual is split into two runbooks that share one section numbering (so `§8b` means the same section in either): `docs/runbooks/devcontainer-sandbox.md` carries day-to-day operation (credential rule §0, getting in §1, lifecycle §2, egress triage §3, engine seam §5, running git §7d, credential injection, collected foot-guns), while `docs/runbooks/devcontainer-sandbox-lifecycle.md` carries recreating, resizing, verifying and upgrading (§7b templates, §7e full disk, §7f the `sbx run` false failure, §8 disk sizing, §8b cold recreate, §10 the harness, §10b the `sbx` version and upgrade ritual). The lifecycle file was split out of the main runbook on 2026-10-10 (item #682) so each source stays small enough for the wiki generator; the section numbers are unchanged.

The `sbx` v0.44–v0.47 release-note items that affect this environment are narrow and none widens egress: `sbx rm` prompts in v0.45.0 and declining returns non-zero, so scripts and agent shells need `--force`; egress became stricter across v0.45.0–v0.47.0 (DNS resolution is refused when no rule permits it, PTR lookups only for already-authorized IPs, policy-evaluation failures fail closed, and raw TCP to a denied hostname is no longer let through by an allow rule for its resolved IP); and `sbx create` still has no `--disk` flag on v0.47.0, so disk sizes remain creation-time environment variables.

The verified 2026-10-08 upgrade to `sbx` v0.47.0 plus the 150 GB recreate passed the harness at 12/12 (including `reproducible-recreate`), the G5 sibling-egress refusal, and the host-side `verify-sandbox-egress.sh --audit-check` with all 50 canonical destinations live in the policy; the volumes were confirmed from the host at `mcm-docker.img` 150.0 GB and `rwlayer.img` 40.0 GB. The first harness run was 9/12, with three failures that were not regressions: the refusal-body marker change (an instrument fault), the personal layer absent on a CLI `devcontainer up`, and a known first-run `firewall-allowlist` case that passed on re-run.

Android emulator support is path-dependent and documented as a three-row matrix: never on the Docker Sandbox microVM (no nested virtualization, so `/dev/kvm` cannot exist however the container is configured), available headless with hardware acceleration on the retained Docker Desktop / DinD container via the host's `/dev/kvm`, and available in CI — which is the recommended route for agent mobile flows because local Metro OOM-crashes after roughly one to two `/run` calls. `scripts/devcontainer-android.sh` refuses legibly on the sandbox, naming the absence, the reason and both remaining routes, rather than failing as if the image were broken.

The dev environment has two separate devcontainer configs — `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json` for the Docker Desktop / DinD path and `.devcontainer/sandbox/devcontainer.json` for the sandbox microVM path — and they are duplicates rather than an extension: the sandbox variant carries its own `containerEnv`, `runArgs` and `onCreateCommand`, so a change made only to the Docker Desktop file is committed and inert on the path in daily use (FR-032 will collapse them).

Verification of the sandbox environment is a harness rather than a judgement: `.devcontainer/verify/run-harness.sh` enumerates twelve verify scripts by name across three vantage points (in-container, VM-side, host-side), counts any script that produces no explicit pass as a failure, and refuses to report the host-side engine-seam result without `MCM_HOST_CHECK`. It is not read-only — the final check, `verify-reproducible-recreate.sh`, removes the dev container and its derived image by design, so a failure there means the container is already gone rather than that a future recreate would fail.

`.devcontainer/assert-egress-governed.sh` runs from `postStartCommand` and verifies rather than re-implements egress enforcement: it fails if a non-allowlisted host is reachable or if an allowlisted one is not, because a severed network must not read as a security pass. It inherits the restart blindness of any postStart hook — it does not re-run after a Docker-level restart, and it is a creation/attach-time assertion rather than a continuous monitor. The continuous guarantee is the host-side sandbox policy, which survives restarts because it lives outside the VM; `.devcontainer/verify/verify-firewall-allowlist.sh` re-asserts it on demand.

Local service bring-up is identical on both dev-environment paths: `pnpm nx up-auth infrastructure-as-code` (Keycloak + Postgres) first, optionally `pnpm nx up-mcm infrastructure-as-code`, then `cd frontend/mcm-app && pnpm start`; stack profiles and endpoints are documented in `docs/runbooks/local-dev.md`.

Disk is a creation-time concern on the sandbox: two dev-container images (~14 GB toolchain plus ~13.5 GB derived) will not fit at once, so re-pinning means removing the previous pair; sizes come from the creation-time environment variables `DOCKER_SANDBOXES_DOCKER_SIZE` / `DOCKER_SANDBOXES_ROOT_SIZE` (there is no `--disk` flag on v0.47.0), so a resize means recreate. A full disk does not announce itself — it presents as apt signature errors or `exporting layers` failures — and `df` is the authority while `docker system df` over-reports reclaimable space.

The remaining pre-work gate classes beyond the four detailed on the repository page are owned by the pages that document them: instrument-before-belief checks (a tool's "no" is about the tool, and a skipped test reads as a pass) belong to the E2E testing runbook, and "it can't run in this environment" needs the same proof as "it passes" — a credential-driven skip is almost always a missing file rather than a missing capability, so the missing input must be named before a tier is retired to CI; the test tiers to run must be derived from what the diff touches (a tier nobody thought of is a tier that did not run) and a guard that fails because the thing it protects was changed must be updated at the cause rather than deleted, since a guard removed for being inconvenient is the regression it was written to catch; and Renovate's silence is not idleness — routine branch work only happens inside the Friday window (`* 2-4 * * 5`), the nightly cron runs outside it and carries only schedule-exempt security work, and a channel whose lockfile toolchain is missing has its `execa` rejection suppressed to a single dashboard line while producing nothing, every run.

Both devcontainer configs reference their Dev Containers feature by a floating tag, so the real pin is the committed `devcontainer-lock.json` beside each config: the CLI re-resolves the tag to a concrete digest on every build and rewrites the lock file, which is tracked in git on purpose as the supply-chain control. A rebuild that rewrites it with the same digest leaves a clean tree, while a lock file showing as MODIFIED is the intended signal that upstream moved the tag and must be reviewed rather than discarded.

The sandbox config sets `updateRemoteUserUID: true` explicitly rather than relying on its implicit `true` default, because an implicit default that silently no-ops is indistinguishable from one that worked; the thin-layer `Dockerfile` header records that the mechanism was set and rebuilt on that path and `coder` stayed 1001, which is why the working fix lives in `toolchain.Dockerfile` (creating `coder` at 1000:1000 by moving the base image's `node` to 1100) and `fix-workspace-ownership.sh` is retained as the repair that runs at create and at every start.

The README presents exactly two supported environments: the dev container on a Docker Sandbox microVM is the DEFAULT — it carries the entire toolchain and is what the project is developed in day to day — and the native host toolchain is the alternative, needed only for the Android emulator and native mobile builds, which the microVM cannot host.

The native host toolchain prerequisites are Node.js 24 with pnpm (via Corepack) and Nx, Rust pinned to 1.98.0 by `rust-toolchain.toml` (which `rustup` reads automatically for every `cargo`/`rustc` call in the repo, so there is no channel to choose), Python 3.14 + `uv` for the agent layer, Docker Desktop, and Android Studio + JDK 17 for mobile development only; setup is `pnpm install` plus one-time-per-machine shared Docker networks (backend, keycloak, movie-assistant-mcp), four named volumes, and `node scripts/gen-dev-secrets.mjs`.

The prebuilt `mcm-devcontainer` toolchain image bakes Rust and its cargo tooling, Python via `uv`, the Specify CLI, Node 24 / pnpm / Nx, and `gh`, so nothing is reinstalled per session; it is pulled from the forge registry by digest or built locally with `node scripts/build-devcontainer-image.mjs`.

The headless entry point into the sandbox environment runs inside the VM, where the engine and the workspace clone live: `ssh mcm.sbx` followed by `devcontainer up --workspace-folder /workspaces/mcm --config .devcontainer/sandbox/devcontainer.json`.

The current pinned tech stack is Expo SDK 57 / React Native 0.86 / React 19.2 on the universal client, Rust 1.98 (channel 1.98.0) on the backend, Node 24 for the BFF container and the dev-container toolchain image, with pnpm 12 workspaces and Nx 23 orchestrating JS/TS, Rust and Python through one task runner. The Node pin is deliberately not single-sourced: the workflow `node-version:` entries, the app Dockerfile's `FROM node:` and the bare `24` in the infra-image-scan workflow are allowed to differ, so the version must be read per context rather than quoted once.

How the Expo app is developed from inside the dev container is path-specific: the web target runs `pnpm start` in-container against the forwarded `localhost:8081` (ports 8081 Metro/web/dev-BFF, 8082 containerized BFF and 8099 Keycloak are forwarded, while the legacy Expo 19000/19001/19006 ports are unused by SDK 57); a physical device points Expo Go or a dev build at the in-container Metro server over LAN, falling back to the documented Expo tunnel (`pnpm start --tunnel`) when LAN routing to the container is unavailable; and emulator/native work — `expo run:android`, APK builds, `pnpm nx e2e:mobile` — stays off the sandbox.

The package manager and task runner are pinned exactly and single-sourced: pnpm 12 via the root manifest's `packageManager` field and Nx 23.3.0 with its plugins at the same version, while the repository's Node floor stays at `engines.node >= 22.13` even though pnpm 12 declares only `>=18`. `scripts/check-toolchain-consistency.mjs` enforces the floor across every workflow and Dockerfile Node pin, requires any other named pnpm version to match `packageManager`, and rejects a second `packageManager` field outside the root manifest because corepack resolves that field from the nearest manifest and a duplicate silently wins in its directory.

ESLint 10's flat config replaced the legacy eslintrc format in both linted projects: `frontend/mcm-app/.eslintrc.json` and `packages/design-system/.eslintrc.json` are gone, replaced by an `eslint.config.js` in each, and the app's lint target now runs `eslint src` with no `--ext`. The flat configs globally ignore the JS/MJS/CJS extensions (flat config lints them by default and cannot narrow extensions from the CLI, so the old linted TypeScript set is preserved), wrap the Expo flat preset in `fixupConfigRules` from `@eslint/compat` because `eslint-config-expo`'s bundled react and import plugins still peer ESLint ≤ 9 and call context methods ESLint 10 removed, and pin four rules to the ESLint 8 resolved behaviour for parity. `nx.json`'s lint target inputs accept both `.eslintrc*` and `eslint.config*`, so lint cache keying survived the rename.

The design system's UI styling library (Tamagui) is on v3 at one exact version in both workspace manifests with no compiler plugin, and `scripts/__tests__/tamagui-version-lockstep.guard.test.mjs` pins that shut: every `tamagui`/`@tamagui/*` specifier must be an exact version and both manifests must agree, the lock must hold a single `@tamagui/core` and `@tamagui/web`, the removed v2 Babel compiler plugin must be named nowhere, and every such update must resolve into one Renovate group so the bot cannot propose half the set. The guard exists because a lockfile refresh had already dragged a v3 core in beside the v2 packages through an open `>=` devDependency with no Renovate PR and no review.

Feature 081 takes every major dependency the bot proposes to a decided end state — upgraded, or held with a measured reason and a re-check rule — one stage per pull request in a fixed order. Majors that cannot land are stopped in `renovate.json` rather than left to propose weekly: keyed security overrides in `pnpm-workspace.yaml` have `major` updates disabled because the npm manager reads the override value as a direct range and would widen its cap to the newest major, and each SDK- or lint-pinned held toolchain major gets its own group behind a `dependencyDashboardApproval` tick, since renovate@44 sets a branch's approval flag from `upgrades.some(...)` and one tick would otherwise release every held js major at once.

Feature 080 replaced the from-source object-store image with an upstream, digest-pinned `rustfs/rustfs` Docker Hub pull in the observability stack and the backup stack, so the object store is now scanned by the ordinary infra-image CVE sweep like every other third-party server image instead of by a workflow of its own; the data moved onto a new external volume in a one-way migration whose old format is not readable by the new store.

The repository's dependency pins must be re-derived from the declaring manifests — `frontend/mcm-app/package.json` and `packages/design-system/package.json` for the universal client, `backend/mc-service/Cargo.toml` plus `rust-toolchain.toml` for the backend, `package.json` and `nx.json` for the package manager and task runner, and `agents/movie-assistant/pyproject.toml` (the `requires-python` floor, mirrored in `uv.lock`) plus `agents/movie-assistant/Dockerfile` (the Python 3.14 runtime image) for the agent layer — because the README's tech-stack table is a human-readable overview whose section and line range move as the document is edited, so a line-range citation of it goes stale while the facts it stated remain true.

Node is the one toolchain version the repository deliberately does not single-source, and the gate enforces a floor rather than agreement: `scripts/check-toolchain-consistency.mjs` fails only when a Node pin is below the root manifest's `engines.node` floor or is not an explicit version, never merely because two pins differ. The accepted consequence is that a Node bump can arrive as two Renovate PRs on two channels (`ci actions` for workflow `node-version:`, `docker base images` for Dockerfile `FROM node:`). The floor is a compatibility statement rather than a pin — every pin runs 24.x — and it must be raised whenever `packageManager` moves to a manager with a higher floor, or the gate keeps passing pins that manager refuses to run on.
